# Copilot instructions for GumTree

## Build, test, and lint

Use the Gradle wrapper from the repository root. The build targets Java 17 and the wrapper supplies Gradle 9.7.1.

```bash
# Build, test, Checkstyle, and package all subprojects
./gradlew build

# Run all verification tasks without assembling distributions
./gradlew check

# Run every test
./gradlew test

# Run one module's tests
./gradlew :core:test

# Run one test class or one test method
./gradlew :core:test --tests com.github.gumtreediff.test.TestDiff
./gradlew :core:test --tests 'com.github.gumtreediff.test.TestDiff.someTestMethod'

# Run Checkstyle for a module
./gradlew :core:checkstyleMain :core:checkstyleTest

# Build the runnable GumTree distribution
./gradlew :dist:shadowDistZip
```

Tests use JUnit Jupiter. The common `java-conv` convention in `buildSrc` applies Java 17, JUnit Platform, and the repository Checkstyle configuration (`gumtree_checkstyle.xml`, with suppressions in `checkstyle_ignore.xml`) to the Java modules. `gen.srcml` uses the external-test convention, so its tests are skipped unless the required `srcml` executable is installed and `-PtestExternal` is supplied:

```bash
./gradlew -PtestExternal :gen.srcml:test
```

The CI workflow also runs the dataset benchmarks and notebook analysis. Benchmark tasks accept comma-separated matcher IDs and an optional limit; run only selected datasets when possible:

```bash
./gradlew :benchmark:listMatchers
./gradlew :benchmark:runBenchmark -Pbenchmarks=d4j,bip -Pmatchers=simple,classic -Plimit=10
./gradlew :benchmark:analyzeBenchmark
```

The benchmark datasets are external inputs and may not be present in every checkout. The analysis report is generated by Java and does not require a Python installation.

## Architecture

GumTree is a Gradle multi-project Java application:

- `core` is the reusable differencing engine. It owns the tree model and I/O, tree generators, matchers and mapping stores, edit-action generation, and core algorithms.
- `gen.*` projects provide language-specific tree generators. Most depend on `core`; JavaParser, JDT, Rhino, CSS, JSON, XML, YAML, and Tree-sitter-NG are in-process generators. `gen.srcml` adapts the external `srcml` process, while `gen.antlr3` and `gen.antlr4` provide shared grammar/build support.
- `client` defines the command-line client framework and `client.diff` supplies diff clients and views (text, HTML/web, Swing, DOT, and directory comparison).
- `dist` assembles the runnable CLI using `com.github.gumtreediff.client.Run` as its application entry point. Its Shadow distribution packages the selected generators and clients into the GumTree command-line archive.
- `benchmark` is a separate runner over Defects4J, GitHub Java/Python, and BugsInPy datasets and can generate a standalone HTML analysis report.

The project graph is declared in `settings.gradle`. New modules must be included there; a generator or client also needs to be added to the relevant `dist` dependencies if it is expected to be available in the packaged CLI.

## Repository-specific conventions

- Update `CHANGELOG.md` when a change is user-visible or otherwise relevant to project release notes. Add the entry under the appropriate unreleased or version section and follow the existing changelog style; do not add entries for internal-only refactoring, tests, or documentation changes unless they affect users or contributors.
- Use Conventional Commits for commit messages: format them as `<type>[optional scope]: <description>` (for example, `fix(core): handle empty trees`). Use an appropriate type such as `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, or `chore`; add a body or breaking-change footer when useful.
- Runtime discovery is annotation-driven. Generator classes use `com.github.gumtreediff.gen.Register` with an ID and accepted filename patterns; matchers and clients have analogous `@Register` annotations. `client.Run` uses ClassIndex to discover subclasses and install them into the registries at startup. Preserve unique IDs, accepted extensions/patterns, and registration annotations when adding implementations.
- A generator is normally a small `gen.*` project layered on `core`; keep language parsing and conversion there rather than adding language-specific behavior to core. Follow the existing project convention files in `buildSrc` and declare the `core` project dependency explicitly.
- The packaged CLI relies on Shadow's merged service metadata and the `dist` dependency graph. If a new registered implementation is not present in `dist`, it may work in its module tests but will not be discoverable from the distribution.
- Tests are colocated with each module under `src/test/java`, and parser/generator tests commonly use fixture inputs under `src/test/resources`. Keep language-specific fixtures and assertions with their generator module; keep algorithm and tree-model tests in `core`.
- External-process tests are intentionally opt-in through `-PtestExternal`; do not make normal `build` depend on locally installed tools.
- Benchmark selection is configured through Gradle properties: `-Pbenchmarks` (or `-Pdatasets`) chooses datasets, `-Pmatchers` chooses matcher presets/IDs, and `-Plimit` caps cases. Use the task aliases documented by `:benchmark:tasks` rather than hard-coding dataset runner arguments.
- CI runs `./gradlew build` together with selected benchmark runners and `:benchmark:analyzeBenchmarks`; changes affecting benchmark inputs, matcher behavior, or generated reports should account for that workflow.
